results.summary_before: This design displays a simple snake pattern on a 7-segment display, advancing with each clock cycle. It was created during a Wokwi workshop and requires an external 7-segment indicator, with the decimal point unused. The design lacks reset logic, so the initial state is unpredictable, and it has no debounce, meaning a physical button clock source will not work reliably. It uses one input for the clock and eight outputs for the display segments.

results.summary_before: This project explores a delta-sigma ADC implemented digitally using flip-flops as quantizers and switched-capacitor lines for reference and measurement. It outputs pulse-density modulated signals and filtered 13-bit values, with a difference output representing the ADC code. The design requires external capacitors, resistors, and a current source/sink for operation. It aims to evaluate PVT effects and mismatch on ADC linearity, with an effective resolution of 11 bits.

results.summary_before: This design is a variable-delay chain intended for setup timing violation and glitching experiments. It contains eight delay chains, each with nine stages holding 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 96, and 128 inverter pairs, selectable via a test control input. Measurements require a carefully controlled glitchy clock, such as one generated by a ChipWhisperer, to arm and measure the delay line and observe setup violations. The module is aimed at evaluating the impact of place-and-route, temperature, and voltage on timing violations.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design is a write-only SPI peripheral that drives WS2812B RGB LED matrices or strips, latching each 3-byte GRB frame to the next LED in sequence. It operates with SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz and supports roughly 300 Hz refresh for an 8x8 matrix. Testing involves connecting a Pi Pico as SPI master and running an example MicroPython script, with optional status LEDs for debugging. Up to 64 LEDs have been tested, and the design requires an external WS2812B matrix or strip plus an SPI master.

results.summary_before: This is a testchip containing a 16x32 single-port OpenRAM SRAM macro that uses two-phase clocking to avoid hold violations. It includes a scan chain for testing and supports byte write masking via the bidirectional pins. The design operates at clock frequencies up to 250 MHz and is controlled through dedicated inputs for clocks, chip select, write enable, and scan signals. No external hardware is required, but a scan chain tester may be used to verify functionality.

results.summary_before: This design is an RGBW color processor that converts SPI commands into four PWM channels for driving LEDs, with a color wheel mode that generates hue, tint, and intensity from a color index. It operates as an SPI slave in Mode 0 and can also directly map RGBW values to PWM outputs in bypass mode. Testing is typically done with a MicroPython script on the Tiny Tapeout demoboard, and external hardware consists of four LEDs connected to the output pins with current-limiting to avoid exceeding 4 mA per pin. The design is notable for its flexibility in controlling RGBW LEDs and its provision of test outputs for debugging, but it requires careful handling of output current.
